BAR for rust-5 (written 2026-10-03 before any run). This is a BAR: it can come out against Rust, for Rust, or as a tie. Expected values are written below so a surprise is visible.

 RULE A AND HOSTS (verifier pass 2026-10-03). LOG.md 2026-09-12 14:16Z ruled box2 timing INADMISSIBLE (Rule A: timing numbers only on box1) and state/BOXES.md reads box1 "NO timing numbers until CPUQuota/thermal checked" and box2 "NO timing numbers (Rule A)"; box3 is the same CPU as box2. The ONLY labelled host is box1 (tiers T0 and T1); box2 (T0) and box3 (T0) are reported with no label ("informal per Rule A"). RESEARCH_LOOP.md E6 treated a quiet box1 as Rule-A legal timing iron. Before registration the registrar checks box1 CPUQuota and thermal state while idle, records the dated result and gets BOXES.md updated (spot read only, not the check: 2026-10-04 00:12Z cm-tick CPUQuotaPerSecUSec=infinity, thermal zones 25 to 30 C, load 1.68 from other jobs). A written Fable or Justin ruling admitting box2 may reinstate it as a labelled host by amend-bar before start only.

ANSWERS (two separate answers, never merged):
 LANGUAGE (part A): our Rust inner loop against our C inner loop, same algorithm, same compiler effort, bit-equal output required.
 KERNELS (part B): our strict-order inner loops against library kernels (OpenBLAS, MKL inside torch, ggml). Speed only; the arithmetic differs and the result sentence says so. Part B is not a statement about the Rust language.

QUESTION. For one dense fp32 matrix-vector product with the 4-row interleaved summation order, does Rust compile to faster, level or slower code than C (language), and how far are our strict-order loops from the library kernels (kernels)?

ALGORITHM (fixed now). y[i] = sum over k = 0..K-1 of W[i,k] * x[k], accumulated per row strictly left to right in fp32 (no fused multiply-add, no reassociation, no pairwise sums), rows processed in groups of 4 with four independent accumulators (for each k: acc[r] += W[4g+r,k] * x[k] for r in 0..4). W row-major fp32 aligned to 64 bytes, x and y fp32. Shapes M x K: 576x1536, 576x576, 1536x576 (the 135M model shapes), 2048x2048 and 256x256 (cache-resident). CACHE REGIME (stated now): fp32 weight working set per shape is 576x1536 = 3.4 MiB, 576x576 = 1.27 MiB, 1536x576 = 3.4 MiB, 2048x2048 = 16 MiB, 256x256 = 0.25 MiB. Box1 (i5-5200U) has a 3 MB L3, so 576x1536, 1536x576 and 2048x2048 exceed it, 576x576 fits in L3 and 256x256 fits in the L2 and L3 range. Box1 peak single-thread sequential read was measured at 2.93 GB/s (RESEARCH_LOOP.md E6, 2026-09-04), while one strict add chain at about one element per cycle wants about 8.8 GB/s at 2.2 GHz (ESTIMATE), so the three large shapes are expected to be memory-bound and Part A on them is expected to read TIE by construction; 256x256 is the compute-bound shape. The result records for every shape and host whether it is memory-bound or compute-bound (achieved GB/s against the 2.93 GB/s figure, and the in-cache 256x256 rate). Inputs: 5 fixed pseudo-random weight and vector sets from a stored seed (files hashed). Source: plain loops in both languages (arrays of 4 accumulators), no intrinsics, no inline assembly. BOUNDS CHECKS (fixed now): the Rust kernel indexes with get_unchecked inside one unsafe block after one up-front assertion of the dimensions, so Rust and C both run without per-element checks (same effort); the unsafe lines are counted and the result states them. A safe-iterator variant (slices and zip, bounds checks elided by the compiler; objdump lists any panic_bounds_check left in the inner loop) is built as an extra and reported with no label, to show what safety costs. Hand-written AVX2 intrinsic versions are out of scope here (three Rust rewrites already lost to our own kernel, R/2026-09-07-KERNEL-V4-V5-NEGATIVE.md); the aegis tmv_i8_avx2 kernel is a ternary-weight by int8 kernel for the 2B model and is not part of this bar.

ARMS FOR PART A. Rust: rustc version recorded, opt-level 2 and 3 both built, lto fat, codegen-units 1, panic abort, RUSTFLAGS recorded, target-feature -fma. C: gcc version recorded, -O2 and -O3 both built, -mno-fma -ffp-contract=off, no -ffast-math; clang -O3 as an extra, reported only. Per host and tier the Rust reference is the faster of its two levels and the C reference is the faster of its two levels (rule fixed now, applied mechanically to the medians). Tiers: T0 baseline x86-64 (SSE2 only; on every host); T1 AVX2 without FMA (box1 only; `-mavx2` for C, `-C target-feature=+avx2,-fma` for Rust). On hosts without AVX2 the T0 comparison is LLVM autovectorisation against GCC autovectorisation of the same loop, and the result says that. Both kernels are built as static libraries with one C ABI and no inlining across the boundary, and are timed from ONE harness (C) through the same function pointer, so timing code is identical. objdump of each kernel is checked: any FMA instruction makes that build INVALID.
Correctness gate: the output y of Rust and C is compared with memcmp on all 5 input sets on every host and tier, and against a plain single-row left-to-right reference. Any difference makes that host and tier INVALID (a correctness finding, recorded).

ARMS FOR PART B (speed only; arithmetic differs: these are vectorised across k and may fuse, so no bit-equality exists and none is required).
 K1 OpenBLAS cblas_sgemv, library version and core type recorded, OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1. K2 torch.nn.functional.linear fp32 (MKL), torch 2.14.0+cpu, torch.set_num_threads(1), a batch of one vector, MKL_VERBOSE kept (on box2 and box3 the dispatch line is recorded). The K2 loop runs 2000 (200) calls inside torch.inference_mode() with preallocated tensors and is timed as one block with time.perf_counter_ns, so per-call Python and dispatch overhead is INCLUDED in K2 and is not subtracted; its floor is measured by the same loop on a 1x1 linear and printed next to K2, and the K2 sentence says "includes Python dispatch". K3 ggml fp32 (entry point named now): a graph built once with ggml_mul_mat(ctx, W, x), W an F32 tensor with ne = [K, M] and x an F32 tensor with ne = [K, 1], run with ggml_graph_plan and ggml_graph_compute at n_threads = 1 from a small harness linked to the pinned llama.cpp build (commit hash recorded); graph build and buffer allocation sit outside the timed loop. Reported with no label, "different precision and arithmetic": K4 ggml Q8_0 dot (32-element blocks, fp16 scales), K5 torch dynamic int8 linear if available. Our side is the faster of the Rust and C T0 or T1 kernels on that host (the tier matching the library's ISA is recorded; on box1 the LABELLED comparison is T1 against the libraries and T0 against the libraries is reported with no label; on the other hosts T0, reported).

METRIC AND STATISTIC. ns per matrix-vector call: per-rep value = mean over 2000 calls (200 calls for 2048x2048; 2000 for 256x256) after 5 untimed warm-up reps; statistic = median of 20 per-rep values per arm, per shape, per host, per tier; arm order rotated every rep; one core, pinned with taskset, one thread; call results consumed through a checksum so nothing is removed. Speed ratio r = 1 / ns ratio (higher speed is better).

LABELS (no gaps, no overlaps).
 PART A per shape. r = (C median ns) / (Rust median ns), i.e. Rust speed over C speed. RUST AHEAD: r > 1.05 and every Rust per-rep value is faster than every C per-rep value. TIE: 0.95 <= r <= 1.05 (both boundaries are TIE). RUST BEHIND: r < 0.95 and every C per-rep value is faster than every Rust per-rep value. INCONCLUSIVE: r outside 0.95 to 1.05 with overlapping rep ranges; redone once with 40 reps; if the ranges still overlap the label is TIE (NOT SEPARABLE).
 PART A per host and tier (5 shapes; A = number of shapes labelled RUST AHEAD, B = number labelled RUST BEHIND; a shape that stays TIE (NOT SEPARABLE) after the redo counts as TIE, so it adds to neither): RUST AHEAD if A >= 3 and B = 0; RUST BEHIND if B >= 3 and A = 0; LEVEL if A = 0 and B = 0; LEANS RUST AHEAD (<A> of 5 shapes ahead, the rest TIE) if A is 1 or 2 and B = 0; LEANS RUST BEHIND (<B> of 5 shapes behind, the rest TIE) if B is 1 or 2 and A = 0; MIXED if A >= 1 and B >= 1 (per-shape labels quoted, no single label). The six cases cover every (A, B). Hosts and tiers are never merged.
 PART B per library and shape, speed only. q = (library median ns) / (our median ns), i.e. our speed over the library's. OURS AHEAD: q > 1.10 and non-overlapping reps. TIE: 0.90 <= q <= 1.10. OURS BEHIND: q < 0.90 and non-overlapping reps. Overlap: redone with 40 reps, then TIE (NOT SEPARABLE). Per library and host the five shapes combine by the same A, B rule as part A (OURS AHEAD, OURS BEHIND, LEVEL, LEANS OURS AHEAD, LEANS OURS BEHIND, MIXED). Labels are given for K1, K2, K3 only.

TRUST COLUMN. Exact equality of Rust and C outputs on every host (the gate above); unsafe lines per kernel; Part B arms carry "arithmetic differs".

EXPECTED (ESTIMATE, before any run). Part A, T0: LEVEL about 55 percent, RUST BEHIND about 25 percent, RUST AHEAD about 20 percent; the strict order forbids vectorising across k, so both compilers will pack no more than the four row accumulators. T1 on box1: same split. Part B: OURS BEHIND for K1, K2 and K3 about 70 percent per host label. The factor 2 to 8 applies to the cache-resident shapes (256x256, 576x576) where kernels are compute-bound (library kernels vectorise across k with fused multiply-add; our fixed order is the price of identical bits across CPUs, and the result sentence says that). On the memory-bound shapes a library is bandwidth-limited too, so the gap there is expected under 2 and OURS LEVEL is possible (ESTIMATE; the earlier 85 percent and 2 to 8 figure did not allow for the cache regime). K2 also carries Python dispatch overhead. A Part A result far from LEVEL is flagged SURPRISE. Part A on the three memory-bound shapes is expected TIE by construction (about 75 percent); any RUST AHEAD or BEHIND there is flagged SURPRISE.

INVALID (affected host, tier or part gets no verdict; redo): outputs not bit-equal; an FMA instruction in a kernel; host load 0.3 or more before or after; a kept rep with clock drop above 15 percent (three discards make that host INVALID); a library arm run with more than one thread (check /proc status); kernel call removed by the compiler (checksum missing); different inputs between arms (hash).

FIXED NOW (may not change after the initial timing run): the algorithm, the shapes, the inputs, tiers, the harness design, 20 reps and the redo with 40, bands, the faster-of-two-levels rule, the A, B combination rule over 5 shapes, labelled host box1 (T0 and T1; box2 and box3 T0 reported, Rule A), the bounds-check handling, the named K2 and K3 entry points, MemoryMax, the sentences. Recorded and frozen at the initial timing: versions and flags.

HOSTS AND MEMORY. Labelled host: box1 (T0 and T1). Reported with no label (Rule A): box2 (T0) and box3 (T0, N4020), box4 (SSE3) and box5 (SSSE3) with Rust and C only (Rust is a static musl cross-build made on penguin, C builds with the box's own gcc; no torch there; OpenBLAS only if a static build runs). Penguin builds only. MemoryMax box1 4.5 GB, box2 and box3 2.8 GB, box4 and box5 80 percent of free -m total.

SENTENCES.
 Part A: "LANGUAGE (Rust against C, fp32 dense dot, 4-row interleaved, bit-equal output, <tier> on <host>): the Rust kernel is <ahead of | level with | behind> the C kernel on <n> of 5 shapes (<memory-bound | compute-bound> shapes named); host label <RUST AHEAD | LEVEL | RUST BEHIND | LEANS RUST AHEAD | LEANS RUST BEHIND | MIXED>. On hosts without AVX2 this compares LLVM and GCC autovectorisation of the same loop. It says nothing about library kernels."
 Part B: "KERNELS (speed only, arithmetic differs): our strict-order kernel is <ahead of | level with | behind> <OpenBLAS | MKL via torch | ggml F32> on <host>, q=<x>. The library vectorises across k and may fuse; our order is fixed for bit-identity. It says nothing about the Rust language."
title: rust-5: fp32 dense matrix-vector product, 4-row interleaved, Rust vs C same algorithm (LANGUAGE), library kernels as speed only (KERNELS)
